newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS - SLANEY AWAITS ASSURANCES SHE CAN RUN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS - SLANEY AWAITS ASSURANCES SHE CAN RUN.

text.p: Suspended runner Mary Slaney will stay home unless she receives assurances from U.S. track officials that she is eligible to compete in this week's national championships and that other runners will not be affected by her participation, her husband said Tuesday.
"We are concerned about this contamination rule," Richard Slaney said of an IAAF rule that calls for the suspension of athletes who knowningly participate against banned competitors.

"We want assurances that she is eligible to run and that they won't ban other people," Slaney said in a telephone interview for the couple's home in Eugene, Oregon. "If we don't get those assurances, she won't run."

USA Track and Field officials earlier Tuesday declared Slaney an "eligible athlete" for the championships, which begin Wednesday, after receiving a letter from the IAAF saying she was suspended and that she was ineligible to compete either in the United States or internationally until a U.S. hearing is completed on a disputed doping test.
But the U.S. officials stopped short of saying Slaney could compete in the championships. "We are studying our options and procedures," spokesman Pete Cava said.

The IAAF letter was a follow-up to comments IAAF president Primo Nebiolo made 11 days ago, banning Slaney and fellow American athletes Sandra Farmer-Patrick and Stephon Flenoy until their doping cases were resolved by U.S. officials.

In each case the athlete was found last summer to have a higher than acceptable ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone. Any ratio above 6-1 is considered suspicious by the IAAF and an athlete is subject to suspension.
Farmer-Patrick and Flenoy, who has an arbitration hearing on his case Wednesday, have been suspended by the U.S. federation. Slaney has not.

Slaney and Farmer-Patrick have denied taking any substance banned by the IAAF. But IAAF general secretary Istvan Gyulai, reached in Monte Carlo, said: "There is a very clear indication that this (Slaney) is a doping case."
Cava said the IAAF letter also reminded U.S. officials of the "contamination rule" if they allowed Slaney to compete.
"That's not fair," Richard Slaney said. "The other athletes should not be punished. This whole thing is absurd."
Slaney said his wife tentatively has plans to fly to Indianapolis Thursday, a day before her first women's 1,500-meter race.
"But if we don't get those assurances, she won't run, and if she doesn't run, there is no point in coming."

Cava earlier Tuesday had said that the U.S. federation "would invalidate" Slaney's entry for the championships once it received official notification of her suspension by the IAAF. But U.S. officials reversed course later in the day. Cava said the decision to make Slaney "eligible" was made after U.S. officials consulted with counsel Peter Alkaly.

Asked what would happen if the U.S. federation decided to allow Slaney to compete, the IAAF's Gyulai said: "I don't believe any member of the IAAF can ignore the actions of the IAAF. There would be outrage."
Even if the U.S. federation clears Slaney, the IAAF would take the case to arbitration between the two federations, Gyulai said.
